explain.say: In 1896, scientists found that uranium gives off invisible rays. Marie Curie, a Polish scientist working in Paris, decided to study them. Look at the next box: she measured the rays very carefully with a meter that her husband Pierre had helped invent. Why is measuring so important?

faq.q: How did Marie Curie discover radium?
faq.a: She found pitchblende gave off stronger rays than its uranium explained. With Pierre Curie she separated tonnes of ore, tracking the rays, and found radium in December 1898.
Pitchblende is a dark, heavy ore, a rock from which uranium is taken. It also contains tiny amounts of radium and polonium.
asks: What rock did Marie Curie use?

faq.q: Why did Marie Curie win two Nobel Prizes?
faq.a: She shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics for research on radioactivity, and won the 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry alone for discovering polonium and radium.
asks: How many Nobel Prizes did Marie Curie win?

faq.a: Radioactivity is when the centre of an atom breaks down and gives out energy as invisible rays. Marie Curie invented the word.
Yes. Its rays harm living cells. People did not know this at first, and Marie Curie's long work with it likely made her ill. Today it is handled with great care.
asks: Why are Marie Curie's notebooks radioactive?

facts: Marie and Pierre Curie announced polonium in July 1898 and radium in December 1898.
Marie Curie won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903 and in Chemistry in 1911.
